title: How Water Reaches Your Tap
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: In most cities, the water that comes out of a tap began its journey weeks earlier as rain or melted snow. It runs into rivers, lakes and underground stores, and from there it is taken to a treatment plant, where it is made safe to drink. The process takes only a few hours, but it involves several carefully controlled stages, and an error at any stage could make thousands of people ill. For this reason, the quality of drinking water is tested far more often than that of almost any other product that people buy, sometimes as often as every hour.

The first stage is the intake, where water is drawn from a river or reservoir through large pipes. At the entrance, a metal screen removes leaves, fish, plastic bottles and other large objects that would damage the machinery. Some plants also use a pre-treatment tank, where the water rests for a time so that the heaviest sand and stones sink to the bottom. Engineers monitor the flow constantly, because after heavy rain the water can contain ten times more mud than usual, and the plant must adjust its settings quickly to cope with the change.

Next comes coagulation. A chemical, usually a compound of aluminium or iron, is added to the water and mixed quickly. The tiny particles of clay and dirt that make the water cloudy carry a small electric charge, which keeps them apart, but the chemical cancels the charge, and the particles stick together to form larger lumps called flocs. The water then flows slowly into a settling tank, where the flocs, now heavy enough, sink to the bottom as sludge. This can remove up to ninety per cent of the dirt, and the sludge is later pumped away and dried.

The water that remains still contains very small particles, so it is passed through a filter. A typical filter is a deep bed of sand and gravel, with a layer of crushed coal on top. As the water trickles down through it, the particles are trapped between the grains. Every day or two, the filter is washed by pushing clean water upwards through it, which carries the dirt away. Some modern plants use membranes instead of sand; a membrane has holes so small that even bacteria cannot pass through, although it is more expensive to run.

Even clear water may contain bacteria and viruses, so the next step is disinfection. Most plants add a small amount of chlorine, which kills germs and continues to protect the water as it travels through the pipes. Others use ultraviolet light or ozone gas, which work faster and leave no taste, but give no protection once the water has left the plant. Chlorine does have disadvantages: some people dislike its smell, and in rare cases it can combine with natural substances to form harmful compounds, so the amount used must be carefully controlled.

The treated water is finally stored in large covered tanks, often built on hills so that gravity can push it through the pipes to homes and factories. Pumps provide the extra pressure that is needed for tall buildings. A city's pipe network may be many thousands of kilometres long, and in old cities some pipes are more than a century old, so leaks are a serious problem. In some places, as much as a third of the treated water is lost before it reaches the customer, which wastes both money and energy.

Engineers are now looking for ways to make the whole system more efficient. Sensors placed in the pipes can detect a leak within minutes and show where it is, so that crews can repair it before a road collapses. Some cities reuse water from their sewage plants, after treating it so that it is cleaner than the river water it replaces. Dr Hamid Karimi, a water engineer, says that the supply of clean water is one of the great challenges of this century, and that wasting it will soon be seen as a luxury that nobody can afford.
